title: How AI Rewrote the Rules of Engineering Multitasking
author: Karol Wojciszko
summary: An engineering leadership newsletter revisits the classic case for sequential over parallel work -- finishing one two-day task before starting the next ships the first feature in two days versus four, with identical total time invested -- and argues AI coding tools have changed what 'sequential' practically means without invalidating the underlying math. The author's key move is naming and dismantling the psychological trap behind chronic multitasking: starting a new initiative feels like progress because sitting with an unstarted task feels worse than sitting with several unfinished ones, even though starting more doesn't actually move any of them closer to completion, an anxiety-driven instinct rather than an analytical one. Because a large share of coding time is now spent waiting on an AI prompt to finish rather than actively typing, the piece revises the old 'do only one thing' rule into 'still finish before you start, but use the waiting time productively' -- while warning explicitly against letting that waiting-time productivity regress into the old trap of a dozen half-open initiatives. Writing candidly about his own ADHD, the author distinguishes task-switching (which doesn't tire him within the same business domain) from domain-switching (same task type, different project, which resets his mental model completely each time), and describes reorganizing his week around business domains rather than task types as the practical fix, while personally testing and settling on three-to-four parallel AI-assisted threads as his own individually-calibrated limit.
points: The worked math example -- two two-day tasks run in parallel both finish in four days, while run sequentially the first ships in two days and the second in four, for identical total effort -- makes concrete why sequential work outperforms parallel work despite feeling less 'efficient' in the moment.

The essay names the specific psychological trap behind chronic overcommitment: starting something new relieves the anxiety of an unstarted task, even though it does nothing to bring any existing task closer to completion, meaning the instinct to open more threads is anxiety-driven rather than analytically justified.

The AI-era revision to the sequential-work rule is precise and actionable: since most coding time is now spent waiting on a prompt rather than typing, the waste has moved from 'typing while multitasking' to 'staring at nothing while a prompt runs' -- so the fix is using wait time productively, not abandoning sequential discipline altogether.

The ADHD-specific distinction between task-switching (tolerable within one domain) and domain-switching (draining because the underlying mental model resets completely) generalizes into a concrete scheduling fix -- grouping a week by business domain rather than by task type -- that readers without ADHD could still apply to reduce their own context-switching costs.
quotes: Open three initiatives at once, and surely one of them lands sooner. That's the logic I ran on for years, and I still catch myself falling back into it. It doesn't. Run the math, and sequential almost always wins.
The moment something is started, it feels closer to done. That feeling is wrong. The instinct to start more comes from anxiety, not from analysis.

Take two initiatives that each need two days of focused work. Run them in parallel, splitting your attention, and both stretch out to four days. Run them one after another, and the first one ships in two days flat, the second by day four. Same total time. Completely different outcome, because now you have one feature in production after two days instead of zero.
Most of the time spent coding today isn't spent typing, it's spent waiting on a prompt to finish. You write the prompt, and then you sit there. Sitting there is the actual waste.

What wrecks me is the opposite: same task type, different domain. Planning session for project A, straight into a planning session for project B, then project C. The mental model underneath it resets completely every single time.
AI didn't kill the case for sequential work. It just moved the waste from "typing while multitasking" to "staring at nothing while a prompt runs." Fix that, and the old math still holds.
